title: Dying in the Word
hookLine: he speaks of dying to ego through the Word and living truly

cards: Some phrases sound alarming until you see them up close. An argument at the dinner table: someone is sure they're right, and your clever reply is loading. Then, for no reason anyone can see, you let it go.
The reply dies unspoken. Something small in you has to lose for the evening to be saved. Guru Amar Das has a bold phrase for a much larger version of that moment: to die in the Word.
It sounds like an ending. In his hymns it's the start of living.

teach.h: DIES IN THE WORD, DIES NO MORE.
teach.b: In Sri Rag he says it like this, paraphrased: whoever dies in the Word stays dead, and does not die a second time. Through the Word the Lord is found, and love for the Name takes hold.
So what dies? Not the body. Haumai, the ego, the I, I, mine.

The Word, sabad, is the Guru's teaching; dying in it means letting that teaching put something other than me at the center, which ego never allows. Then the strange promise: you don't die a second time.
Some readers take it this way: once ego's grip is broken in the Word, the fear of death and the round of coming and going lose their hold.
Ten days ago, Guru Angad's salok gave this a picture: dying while alive. Sikhs call it jivat marna. It doesn't mean giving up on life, ever.

It means living fully, with the self out of the driver's seat. If dark thoughts about your own life ever come, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Ego rarely dies in one heroic moment.

teach.h: SMALL DEATHS AT THE DINNER TABLE.
teach.b: It dies in dinner-table moments: the reply you don't fire, the credit you don't grab, the grudge you put down.
Each is a small rehearsal of the big thing. And the verse is clear about where this leads. Not into gloom.
What follows the dying is finding the Lord, and a love for the Name that takes hold.

how: Sikhs meet the idea of dying in the Word in Guru Amar Das's hymns, sung in kirtan and explained in katha; it is lived through daily remembrance of the Name and seva done without seeking credit.

games.q: what does “dying in the word” mean?
o: letting ego's grip break through the Guru's teaching
taking a vow of silence and never speaking again
passing away while the Guru's hymns are recited

games.q: dying in the Word: tap the pairs.
p: the ego's grip, not the body
does not die a second time

s: dying in the Word means giving up on life
it means living fully with ego out of the driver's seat, and living truly.
the hymn says whoever dies in the Word does not die a second time
in Sri Rag, Guru Amar Das says they stay dead to ego and do not die again.

games.q: the Guru says: die in the Word. what is it, in his hymns, that dies?
o: the ego's grip, the I, I, mine.
nothing; it's only a figure of speech.
games.why: it's haumai that dies, and the result isn't an ending: through the Word the Lord is found, and love for the Name takes hold.

practice: Find one small want that's mostly about being seen, being right or being first, like the last word in a text thread or someone noticing what you did.
Look at it gently, then on a long breath out set it down, as many times as it takes. If you pray, let Waheguru fill the space it leaves.

wordCard.voice: Dying in the Word. Letting ego's grip break through the Guru's teaching, so that, as Guru Amar Das says, you need not die a second time, and can begin to live truly. Today's word.

orig.note: through the Word: the Guru's teaching, in which, Guru Amar Das says, ego dies.

carryVoice: Your line: die to ego. What lives in its place is the whole point. See you in the morning.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Rag Mahala 3, Ang 58 (sabad marai so mar rahai, phir marai na dooji var)
